newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl denies coalition in trouble over budget.
newsitem.headline: Kohl denies coalition in trouble over budget.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office denied a Sunday newspaper report that his longstanding coalition with the Free Democrats was in deep trouble and the veteran chancellor was struggling to keep it together.
A government spokesman said a report in the Welt am Sonntag which quoted an internal chancellory memo as saying a breakup of the coalition was possible was completely invented.
The spokesman also denied that Kohl was holding long talks at the weekend to try to prevent the Free Democrats (FDP) leaving the ruling group.
But Finance Minister Theo Waigel admitted the atmosphere within the coalition was serious.

"The atmosphere is one of mutual respect and partnership, but it is serious. Each person is aware of their responsibility," ZDF television quoted Waigel as saying in an interview due to be transmitted on Sunday evening.

A Free Democrat spokesman on Saturday denied reports the party had threatened to leave the coalition if it insisted on raising taxes to help get Germany's finances in shape for Europe's single currency.

Waigel on Saturday said he would not resort to raising taxes this year to help plug a shortfall of at least 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in his 1997 budget, but said he could not rule out increases for 1998.
FDP honorary chairman Otto Lambsdorff told German television he was convinced the ruling coalition would not collapse, but stressed his party would not agree to tax hikes.
"Higher taxes would be irresponsible since they would just lead to higher unemployment," Lambsdorff said.

He added that cuts in government spending -- the FDP's favoured solution to Bonn's financial woes -- were necessary not just to help stop budget holes in 1997, but had to be introduced anyway to avoid a similar budget crisis next year.

Slow economic growth and soaring unemployment -- which rose 56,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.358 million in May -- have meant the government is struggling to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product and qualify for membership of a single European currency.
